agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 carries the whole superscription (choirmaster, of David, a psalm) plus the first clause; KJV counts the title as 139:0. I glossed ledavid as 'of David' / 'belonging to David' without deciding authorship, as the preposition lamed is ambiguous.

agent_notes: The last clause is hard. 'Light about me be night' (ASV, BBE) follows Rashi's reading of 'or as darkness; 'night is light about me' (KJV, YLT) takes it as the usual sense. I followed the plain word order, which is ambiguous in Hebrew, and verse 12 settles it. The verb yeshufeni (crush/bruise in Gen 3:15, Job 9:17; cover in Rashi, Radak and Meiri via nashaf 'twilight') is likewise uncertain; I chose 'crush' for the literal layer and 'swallow' for the dramatic, and the commentary lays out the options. Neither choice is certain.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses יַחְשִׁיךְ 'it is [too] dark', which takes the verb as intransitive. The verb is Hiphil of חשך, 'to make dark'. Ibn Ezra and Radak both read it as transitive with an unstated object ('darkness darkens nothing from you'); Metzudat David has the same. The intransitive reading ('is not dark to you') is the other way and is what BBE has. I gloss 'it makes dark' and give the literal layer the transitive form.

(PS.139.12 Ibn Ezra: "פעול יחשיך חסר לא יחשיך דבר ממך"; Radak: "לא יחשיך דבר ממך שלא תראהו".)

agent_notes: קנית (qanita) is glossed 'you acquired/created'; STEPBible has 'created'. The root covers both purchase and creation (Gen 14:19 'maker of heaven and earth'); the literal layer keeps 'acquired' so the ownership sense stays visible, and the commentary explains it. תסכני is read from סכך 'cover, screen' (so Rashi and Ibn Ezra, who equate it with סוכך); a derivation from שׂכך/נסך 'weave' is also proposed by modern lexica, and STEPBible's 'wove together' follows that. I kept 'screened/covered' in the literal layer and noted the weaving reading.

Qere/Ketiv at the end: written ולא 'and not one among them', read ולו 'and to it/him one among them'. The packet's gloss follows the Qere. I translated the Qere in the literal layer and mentioned the Ketiv in the commentary. The sense of the whole clause is contested (days formed, and one of them was his / and none of them yet existed); I chose the Qere sense 'and for it one among them' without resolving it further. גלמי is a hapax; the gloss 'unformed mass' relies on the later usage in rabbinic Hebrew (Metzudat Zion cites 'golmei kli ets', Hullin 25).

history.note: [consider] Either make the dramatic layer follow the Qere or say in the commentary that the dramatic layer takes the Ketiv. (PS.139.16: "וְל֖וֹ (Q(K)) אֶחָ֣ד בָּהֶֽם".)

agent_notes: The packet glosses רעיך as 'thoughts' (רעיון, Aramaic-flavoured רעי). It could also be read as 'your friends' (רֵעֶיךָ from רֵעַ), which is how the Targum and Rashi read it ('the righteous'). I translated 'thoughts', following Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion, and noted the alternative. ראשיהם 'their sum / their totals': Rashi and Radak read as 'totals, main heads' (cf. Ex 30:12).

agent_notes: Addressed the reviewer request: Ibn Ezra and Radak are cited as the readers who take הֱקִיצֹתִי as waking from sleep; Meiri and Metzudat David are grouped as the readers for whom even a sleepless, day-and-night count could not reach the end. Rashi reads it differently again (the end of the generations), and is mentioned only briefly.

אֶסְפְּרֵם is a first-person imperfect; the five English versions split between conditional ('If I should count them', KJV/ASV/Webster/BBE) and YLT's flat 'I recount them'. I kept the literal layer neutral ('I count them') and let the dramatic layer carry the conditional, since the Hebrew has no 'if'.
STEPBible glosses יִרְבּוּן as 'they will be numerous'; I rendered it 'they are more numerous' to keep the comparative sense of מִן ('more than'), which is the natural reading of the מִן + imperfect.

agent_notes: אם here is either an optative ('If only you would slay!', BBE, Rashi) or a conditional with an unspoken conclusion, or 'Surely' (KJV, ASV). Radak and Meiri read it as conditional. I kept it conditional in the literal layer and made it a wish in the dramatic layer, flagged in the commentary. אלוה is the poetic singular of אלהים, glossed 'O Eloah'.

Addressed the review request. Two lines of reading are kept apart. (1) 'They speak of you': Radak takes יאמרוך as ימרוך with the aleph dropped, comparing וְלַעֲמָשָׂא תֹּאמְרוּ (2 Sam 19:14), 'they speak to you / of you according to their scheming'. (2) 'They exalt you': Meiri, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read it from the root of אֶת־יְהוָה הֶאֱמַרְתָּ (Deut 26:17), 'you have declared/exalted', so that the enemies 'exalt' God for the sake of scheming, a hollow lifting up (נשוא לשוא); Metzudat Zion adds that a yod stands for the aleph, as in תִּתְיַמָּרוּ (Isa 61:6). Meiri, in his own words, finds יאמרוך hard because 'saying' is not joined to its object without a ל. I chose the plain 'say/speak' reading in the literal layer and the 'exalt' sense in the dramatic layer only as an undertone; the KJV's 'speak against thee' follows neither reading exactly. The Hebrew has no 'name' in the verse: 'thy name' is a supply in KJV/ASV/Webster (Ibn Ezra and Rashi supply אותך or שמך). עריך is glossed 'your foes' from ער (H6145; cf. 1 Sam 28:16 עָרֶךָ); STEPBible's 'enemies' is kept.

The earlier remark about a written form is removed: nothing in the packet shows a Ketiv/Qere here. אֶתְקוֹטָט is glossed 'I quarrel/loathe'; STEPBible's 'do I loathe' follows the sense of קוּט (Ps 95:10 אָקוּט 'I loathed') as Ibn Ezra reads it, while Radak and Meiri read it as קטטה, 'quarrel'; the five English versions split the same way (KJV 'grieved', YLT 'grieve myself', BBE 'cause of grief'). I took 'quarrel' for the literal layer's second reading in a bracket-free way: 'and with those who rise up against you I contend / loathe'.

agent_notes: BBE paraphrases the verse; KJV 'perfect hatred' translates תכלית 'completeness, end-point'. I kept 'completeness of hatred'.

עֹצֶב is glossed 'idol' by STEPBible (H6090A, the idol sense in Is 48:5 and Ps 16:4 comes from עצב II). Most medieval commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) read it as 'grief/pain/rebellion' (from עצב 'hurt, grieve', Is 63:10). I rendered 'a way of hurt' in the literal layer, with a note on the 'idol' reading; the gloss at pos 4 follows the sense of 'hurt', which I changed from STEPBible's 'idol'. דרך עולם: 'the way of old / everlasting'; Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri also read it as 'the way of death'. I kept 'the way of ancient/everlasting' and noted the death reading.

agent_notes: zerita is disputed. Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David and Ibn Ezra (citing R. Moshe ha-Kohen) derive it from zer 'wreath, border' (encircle), which the KJV 'compassest' follows. STEPBible and YLT ('fanned') take it from zarah 'winnow, sift'. I kept 'sift' in the literal layer and 'encircle' in the dramatic one, and say so in the commentary.

Radak gives two readings. The first (shared by Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Malbim): the word is not yet finished on my tongue and you already know all of it. The second: I plan in my heart to say something, but what my tongue will actually bring out I do not know and you do; he cites Prov 16:1 and calls this reading 'the correct one in my view'. I keep the Hebrew's bare juxtaposition in the literal layer and let the dramatic layer carry the first reading, which is the one most of the commentators and the five English versions share. KJV/ASV/Webster all keep 'For' and add a 'but' the Hebrew lacks; BBE turns the line into 'which is not clear to you'.

history.note: [should_fix] Say that the KJV keeps 'For' and adds a 'but' the Hebrew does not have (an 'except that' reading), and drop the claim that it replaces 'for'. Say that Radak prefers the second reading (God knows what the tongue will say before the speaker does) rather than listing him under the first. (PS.139.4 KJV: "For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O Lord, thou knowest it altogether." Radak: "וזה הפירש הוא הנכון אצלי" (of the second reading, citing Prov 16:1).)

agent_notes: צַרְתָּנִי can come from צור 'besiege, enclose' or from צור 'fashion, form'. Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David and Malbim read siege; Radak reports the reading of his father (Joseph Kimhi) that it is about the shaping of the embryo in the womb. I gloss it 'you enclose me' (STEPBible's gloss) and render 'besieged' in the literal layer, with the second sense in the notes. Rashi's gloss on כַּפֶּכָה is given in the commentary only as a restraint, since his Old French word is hard to read with certainty.
